title: ES Modules, Tree Shaking & High-Performance Architecture
summary: Master ECMAScript Modules (ESM) vs CommonJS, static analysis, bundler tree shaking, and memory leak prevention in long-lived web apps.
learningObjectives: Explain static module analysis and how ES Module structure enables bundlers (Vite, Webpack) to perform dead-code elimination (Tree Shaking)
Identify and eliminate common JavaScript memory leaks (orphaned listeners, detached DOM nodes, uncleaned intervals)

sections.heading: 1. ES Modules (ESM) vs CommonJS & Tree Shaking Mechanics
sections.content:
JavaScript has evolved from ad-hoc script tags and CommonJS (`require()`) to standardized ECMAScript Modules (ESM: `import`/`export`).

Fundamental Differences:
- CommonJS (CJS): Dynamic and synchronous. `require()` can be called conditionally inside if-statements at runtime. Because dependencies are resolved dynamically during execution, bundlers cannot determine which exports are actually used before running the code.
- ES Modules (ESM): Static and asynchronous. `import` statements must reside at top-level. The dependency graph is parsed and resolved BEFORE code execution.

Tree Shaking:
Because ESM imports and exports are completely static, bundlers (Vite, Rollup, Webpack, esbuild) can analyze the module Abstract Syntax Tree and determine with 100% mathematical certainty which functions are never referenced. Unused code ('dead branches') is pruned from the production bundle, slashing network download size.

Memory Leak Prevention in Modern Web Applications:
JavaScript features automatic garbage collection (Mark-and-Sweep). However, memory leaks occur when objects are unintentionally kept reachable from the root window/global scope:
1. Lingering Event Listeners: Attaching listeners to `window` or `document` without removing them when components unmount.
2. Detached DOM Nodes: Retaining references in JavaScript to DOM elements that have been removed from the visible document tree.
3. Uncleared Timers: `setInterval` running indefinitely, referencing closure variables that can never be garbage collected.

codeExamples.code:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| ESM STATIC TREE SHAKING VS DYNAMIC COMMONJS BUNDLING             |
|                                                                   |
|  COMMONJS (require):                                              |
|  Dynamic require("./utils") -> Bundler must include ENTIRE file!  |
|                                                                   |
|  ES MODULES (import { usedFn } from "./utils"):                   |
|  Module Graph (Static):                                           |
|  [utils.js]                                                       |
|    |-- export function usedFn()       ===> Included in Bundle     |
|    |-- export function unusedHeavy()  ===> [PRUNED / TREE-SHAKEN] |
|                                                                   |
|  Production bundle size reduced by eliminating unused functions!  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
codeExamples.explanation: Static ESM syntax allows build tools to discard unused exports during bundling.

keyPoints: ES Modules are static: imports and exports are evaluated at build time before code executes.
Tree shaking removes unused exports, drastically reducing bundle size and browser parse time.
Always unregister event listeners, abort controllers, and timers when tearing down components.
commonMistakes: Exporting single giant default objects ('export default { fn1, fn2 }'), which defeats tree shaking.
Leaving setInterval() running in single-page apps without clearing it on page navigation.

sections.heading: 2. Production Memory Leak Prevention with WeakRef & AbortSignal
sections.content: In modern Single Page Applications (Next.js, React), forgetting to clean up global event listeners is the leading cause of browser tab memory bloat. Using `AbortSignal` allows multiple listeners to be wiped simultaneously with a single abort call.

codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates modern leak-free lifecycle cleanup using AbortSignal to detach event listeners deterministically.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Component mounted: attaching listeners with signal...
Signal aborted: Event listeners detached from memory.
Component unmounted cleanly.

keyPoints: Modern addEventListener accepts an { signal } option, removing the listener automatically when aborted.
WeakMap and WeakRef allow objects to be referenced without preventing garbage collection.
commonMistakes: Using arrow functions in addEventListener and trying to remove them with removeEventListener without saving the function reference.

exercises.title: Audit and Fix a Leaky Timer Component
exercises.objective: Refactor a stateful tracker to implement clean unmount logic and prevent memory leaks.
exercises.description: A dashboard metric widget starts a setInterval heartbeat to fetch telemetry every second. When users switch views, the interval continues running in the background, consuming CPU and retaining stale state. Refactor the widget to provide a start() and dispose() lifecycle that guarantees full resource cleanup.
instructions: Clear any running interval ID inside dispose().
Nullify internal callback references so closures can be collected.
Ensure calling dispose() multiple times is safe and idempotent.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Idempotent cleanup methods ensure background timers are killed and memory references are freed.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why can bundlers tree-shake ES Modules (ESM) but cannot reliably tree-shake CommonJS (require)?

options.text: Because ESM imports and exports are static and can be analyzed at compile time, whereas CommonJS calls can be dynamic at runtime.
Because CommonJS is only supported in Linux environments.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: ESM structure is completely static (top-level only, fixed string specifiers). This allows static AST analysis to identify unused code before runtime.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What is a detached DOM node in JavaScript?

options.text: A DOM element that has been removed from the visible HTML document but is still referenced by a JavaScript variable in memory.
A node created inside an iframe.
A custom HTML tag with a shadow root.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Detached DOM nodes occur when elements are removed from the DOM tree, but JavaScript variables keep referencing them, preventing garbage collection.

recap: Static ES Modules enable tree shaking to minimize bundle sizes. High-performance web apps actively manage memory by cleaning up event listeners, timers, and detached DOM references.
